doc.title: Eric Alexander interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 31, 2010

title: Fewer originals, unusual standards, and High Note radio success
summary: Recent records have few originals and many rarely heard standards, which sell well and reach number one on radio charts.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: That’s one of the reasons that people like Lee Morgan and Hank Mobley wrote ninety percent of the music on their records, and thank God they were incredible writers. And by contrast this is also one of the problems today, everyone wants their mechanicals and everyone thinks they’re a good writer, and most people aren’t. So we see records coming out where you look at it and you say, you know what’s coming, it’s a bunch of stuff that’s not really memorable. So I’m kind of torn. And the last few records I’ve probably stepped too far across the line, I’ve had less originals than ever. I think I’ve had one original or two originals on the last couple of records. And the rest of the tunes are sort of out of the way, rarely heard standards, or strange tunes that people wouldn’t even expect me to record that we rework. But I know that people like that. I know that the listeners like it and the radio stations like it, and so it serves me well in that respect. I know the CDs sell very well, you know, compared to other CDs that my company puts out. And I know that they always get very good radio play. I mean every CD I’ve done for High Note Records has made it to number one on the radio play charts.

Nice. And I agree with what you’re saying. Like you did the tune “It’s Magic,” and it’s exactly what you’re saying when I saw that I go he did “It’s Magic”? Like and then I start to sing the song in my head and I go wow, what an interesting choice. I can’t wait to hear what you did with that.
